cards.explanation: The answer is True. The psalm says it plain: "In my distress I cried to the LORD, and He answered me." (Psalm 120:1) The writer cried out and the LORD answered. That's the whole opening, friends, and everything after it gets told from that spot.

The writer asks to be delivered from lying lips and a deceitful tongue. "Deliver my soul, O LORD, from lying lips and a deceitful tongue." (Psalm 120:2) Notice what the trouble is, friends. It isn't swords or soldiers, it's words that aren't true. I think words like that can sting plenty.

What comes from the warrior is sharp arrows. "Sharp arrows will come from the warrior…" (Psalm 120:4) The song asks the deceitful tongue what will be done to it, and the warrior's arrows show up right after. Whoa, friends. Nobody wants that kind of delivery.

The answer is False. The writer cries, "Woe to me that I dwell in Meshech, that I live among the tents of Kedar!" (Psalm 120:5) Nobody says "Woe to me…" while smiling, friends. Meshech and Kedar are home, but this is no happy home.

The word is hate. The writer says, "Too long have I dwelt among those who hate peace." (Psalm 120:6) So it's not only the place, friends, it's the people around the writer. That would wear anybody down.
The answer is False. The writer says, "Too long have I dwelt among those who hate peace." (Psalm 120:6) Too long is the writer's own word for it, friends. It isn't described as a short while.

The word is war. "I am in favor of peace; but when I speak, they want war." (Psalm 120:7) The writer is in favor of peace, but when the writer speaks, they want war. I think that's a hard spot to be in, friends, and I bet it wears a person out.
